finding.claim: The app takes the caller's identity from the client-supplied request header X-Session-User-Verified. Nothing in the app checks that a trusted proxy set it or that it is signed. The name suggests an upstream proxy sets it, but the app never verifies that. If the app is reachable directly, or the proxy does not strip inbound copies of the header, any client can impersonate any user. That lets them pass the ACL checks on delete and rename for any file whose grants name that user.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled HTTP header X-Session-User-Verified on any request to the Flask app.
finding.sink: acl.is_allowed / ensure_allowed authorization decisions guarding `del STORE[fid]` (delete_file) and `f["name"] = ...` (rename_file).

trace.note: before_request copies the raw header value into g.user with no authentication or verification
is_allowed does a plain lookup of resource['grants'][user], so the spoofed identity string is trusted as-is
the file is deleted once the spoofed identity passes the check
rename_file uses the same g.user for the 'write' check
the file name is overwritten with attacker-supplied JSON

finding.guards_checked: I found no authentication middleware, signature or HMAC check, or token validation in the repo. I found no check on the source IP or proxy, and no code that strips the header. Only views.py and acl.py exist, so I can't see the deployment. The one thing that would mitigate this is an upstream proxy that overwrites the header and an app reachable only through that proxy. The ACL does fail closed when the header is missing: g.user is None and grants.get(None) returns [], unless a grants dict has a None key. Impersonation therefore needs the attacker to know or guess a granted user id, such as the owner's.

verdict.guard_found: none in repo; ACL lookup at acl.py:5 fails closed only for a missing header. Any upstream proxy that strips or overwrites the header is not visible here.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:11 trusts the raw header, views.py:17 and 25 feed it to the ACL checks at acl.py:5 and 10, and the effects land at views.py:18 and 27), but exploitability depends on whether a proxy strips or sets X-Session-User-Verified and whether the app is directly reachable, and neither is visible in views.py or acl.py.

finding.claim: Both routes load the object with STORE[fid] before any authorization check. A nonexistent fid raises KeyError and returns a 500. An existing fid goes on to the ACL check and returns 403 if the caller isn't allowed, so the response distinguishes the two cases. Any caller, including an unauthenticated one, can enumerate valid file ids. Because the 500 is unhandled, it can also add noise to error monitoring. This is low severity.
finding.source: Unauthenticated attacker-chosen fid path parameter on DELETE /files/<fid> and POST /files/<fid>/rename.
finding.sink: Distinguishable responses (500 versus 403) that reveal whether a file id exists.

trace.note: STORE[fid] raises KeyError (500) for an unknown id, before any ACL check
ensure_allowed then returns 403 for an existing id the caller can't use
rename_file does the same lookup before its check, and returns an explicit 403 when the check fails

finding.guards_checked: There is no ordering of authorization before lookup and no uniform 404 or 403 response. There is no errorhandler for KeyError. I am not sure whether debug mode is on, because no run configuration is in the repo. The id's guessability depends on how ids are generated, and that code is not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is tested at views.py:25, but both run only after STORE[fid] (views.py:16, 24). No KeyError handler and no authentication requirement exist.
verdict.reason: views.py:16 and views.py:24 do STORE[fid] before the ACL check, so an unknown fid raises KeyError (500) and a known fid returns 403 via acl.py:10 or views.py:26, which lets any caller, including an anonymous one, tell the two apart. The impact is low: file-id enumeration and error noise only.
